turns.prompt_text: My Bambu lab nozzles are covered in PLA and PETG HF Attached 1 file. - b2b7076f-295e-40bc-a005-7cc1f00da0ce
turns.response_html:
That is quite the buildup you've got there. It looks like those A1-series quick-swap hotends have seen some better days, especially with that PETG HF (High Flow) involved—that stuff is notorious for being "clingy" if the offset is even slightly off.

Cleaning these isn't impossible, but it does require a bit of finesse to avoid damaging the heater or the thermistor wires tucked inside.

The Cleanup Operation

1. The "Hot Wipe" (The First Line of Defense)

If the nozzles are still functional, the easiest way to clean the exterior is heat.

  • Heat it up: Install the nozzle and heat it to about 250°C (or slightly above the PETG HF printing temp).
  • The Tool: Use a brass brush or a thick, folded-over wad of paper towel (be extremely careful not to burn yourself).
  • The Technique: Gently scrub the exterior. Avoid using steel brushes, as they can scratch the nozzle or even short out the heater wires if you're not careful.

2. The Cold Pull (Internal Clogs)

If the flow is restricted, a "cold pull" is your best bet for the PLA.

  • Heat to printing temp, insert filament, then let it cool to about 90°C–100°C for PLA.
  • Quickly yank the filament out. Ideally, it should pull the internal "gunk" out with it in the shape of the nozzle's interior.
  • Note: This is harder with PETG HF as its glass transition temperature is higher; you may need to adjust the "pull" temp to around 120°C for PETG.

3. The "Last Resort" Torch

If the nozzle is completely encased and you can't even get it into the printer:

  • Use a small butane torch to carefully heat the metal body (holding it with pliers).
  • Once the plastic softens to a honey-like consistency, wipe it away.
  • Warning: Do not get the metal glowing red. Overheating can ruin the heat treatment of the stainless steel or damage the internal seals.

Prevention: Avoiding the "Blob of Doom"

To keep this from happening again, especially with high-flow filaments:

  • Check your Silicone Sock: Ensure the silicone socks are clean and properly seated. They are your primary defense against plastic crawling up the heater block.
  • Z-Offset & First Layer: PETG HF is very sensitive to being "squished" too much. If the nozzle is too close to the bed, it will plow through the filament, causing it to curl up and stick to the nozzle.
  • Nozzle Coating: Consider a drop of Slice Engineering Plastic Repellent Paint. It’s like a non-stick coating for your hotend.

The Reality Check

Since these are the A1/A1 mini quick-swap nozzles, they are relatively inexpensive (usually around $10–$15 USD). If the plastic has worked its way into the wiring or if the cleaning process takes you more than 30 minutes, it might be more "cost-effective" for your sanity to simply swap in a fresh one and keep these as "emergency spares" for a rainy day.

Are you seeing any specific error codes on the printer, or is this just a case of "messy nozzle syndrome"?
